title: A pen's blots can be turned off, and a light line blots less
description:
Pen.blots: 1 as now (the default: blots stay on), 0 for a pen that never blots, above 1 for a leaky one. It scales what the ball gathers (the drop it lands with and what a turn leaves), independently of Pen.flow, which today is the only control and darkens the line with it.

Also: blots show on the light side of a hatching. The drop the ball can hold (BALL_BLOB * BALL_INK * flow * bound^2) and what it gathers do not depend on pressure in the way the line does, so a faint line gets blobs as big and dark as a firm one's, which reads wrong. What is gathered and left should go with the pressure of the line (measure a blob's darkness against its line's, at light and firm pressure).

Fits with fusain-azn (the ball blots at every point of a gently curving line) and fusain-uoa (a pen in the hand): do the three together. Alters the picture: record the fingerprint and regenerate the images.
close_reason: Pen.blots scales what the ball gathers (0: never blots); what the paper takes of a drop goes with the pressure of the line: the darkest start against its line 2.60 -> 1.87 at pressure 0.15, 1.38 -> 1.36 at 0.9

title: Soft graphite does not smudge: a stump hardly changes a pencil's tone
description: Found measuring graphite for the lake drawing. Every grade has the same binding (0.85), and a stump only moves dust, so rubbing a 2B tone changed it by a few levels and cut its grain by 10 to 15 per cent; an 8B smudged no more than a 4H; nothing could be dragged out onto bare paper. Real soft graphite rubs smooth under a stump or a finger and drags out; hard leads hardly do. Reproduction: s=Sheet(300,120,seed=1); s.shade((10,10,110,110),pencils.B8,0.9); s.smudge([(20,60),(290,60)],tools.STUMP,0.8) left bare paper at x 130..160 at about 219 against 237.
close_reason: Graphite now slides under a tool that smears (slide_graphite in the rubbing kernel): held graphite is pushed from grain to grain and a little comes loose, the more graphite the lead has. One stump pass leaves 82% of a 4H shading's grain, 74% of an HB's, 57% of a 4B's, 34% of an 8B's; set fixative keeps it; erasers and other media are unchanged. Tests in tests/test_dust.py.

title: Coloured pencil: little takes over a light first layer
description: A light wash of coloured pencil (two or three layers at pressure 0.3 to 0.5) waxes the tooth so far that darker pencils laid afterwards hardly show: in the first examples/macaw.py, deep green and blue over a lime wash left it lime. A coloured pencil artist builds ten or more light layers, light to dark. Measure how many light layers the model takes before it resists, against that practice, and recalibrate WAX_FULL and RESIST (and what a light touch lays) if it is too few.
close_reason: Measured, no recalibration. On cartridge paper, light layers (pressure 0.3) of one pencil take 0.80, 0.58, 0.51, 0.39, 0.36, 0.29, 0.25 of the first and fall to a fifth by the tenth: in line with the ten or more light layers of practice. Over three lime layers a dark pencil takes 0.65 of what it takes on bare paper if they were laid at 0.3, 0.41 at 0.5, 0.25 at 0.75 (which polishes the tooth). The first macaw failed because its washes were pressed up to 0.75. A recalibration (WAX_FULL 0.6, wax piling thicker) gained little and broke 'a waxy lead fills the tooth with less than the same lead without its wax'. Pinned by two tests in tests/test_colour.py; advice added to the README and pencils.py.

title: A full tooth takes hardly any more pastel
description: Once the tooth is full, a further stroke of soft pastel lays next to nothing, and a light stroke over it only catches the grain of the strokes before (shop-window reflections came out as plaid; a red coat over a black car came out striped), unless the layer under it is fixed first. A real soft pastel keeps going on over a full tooth for a while: it is opaque and crumbles on top. The agent drawing examples/broadway.py called fix() every few objects to get round it.
close_reason: Measured, no change to the model. On cartridge and on toned grey paper, layers of soft pastel at 0.7 take 0.70, 0.50, 0.36, 0.25, 0.19, 0.12 of the first: the tooth is full after five or six, as on real pastel paper. White over four layers of black reaches a tone of 0.30 (0.64 over one layer), and 0.56 if the black is fixed first: fixing between stages is what a pastellist does. Pinned by two tests in tests/test_fixative.py; advice in the README. Sanded card holding too little is a separate issue.

title: No way to rub or erase an area
description: Sheet.smudge and Sheet.erase take one path. Rubbing a sky or a shadow face smooth means writing a sweep of strokes by hand, with a mask as the pressure. Wanted: an area form, as Sheet.shade is for media: an area (rectangle or polygon), a tool, a pressure that may be a function of (x, y), an angle. Note: a tool keeps its load across a stretch of no pressure, so a sweep through a mask carries dust over the gaps; the area form should lift the tool there. Found by the agent drawing examples/deco.py.
close_reason: Sheet.rub rubs or erases an area: passes side by side, to and fro, a pressure that may be a function of (x, y), the tool lifted where it is nothing. Tests in tests/test_rub.py.

title: Strokes laid with the side of a stick stay speckled when rubbed
description: Two layers of sheet.shade(box, charcoal.VINE, 0.8, 9, tilt=1) followed by two finger passes stay speckled (pixel std 0.158 at mean 0.62); the same with the point rubs smooth (std 0.113 at mean 0.66). A finger should even out the side of a stick as it does the point. Found by the agent drawing examples/deco.py, which avoided tilt for that reason.
close_reason: A rubbing tool now spreads the dust under it from grain to grain before it is pressed in (spread_dust, SPREAD, SPREADS in _engine.py); tests in tests/test_dust.py.

title: A firm pencil wears a waxed layer away, stroke by stroke
description: Pressed hard over a waxy layer, a tip drags part of the layer along (burnish). What it still carried when the stroke ended left the paper with it, so many short firm strokes wore the layer away. Found drawing examples/macaw.py. Fix: lay what the tip drags on the marked paper under it where it lifts off (set_down in _engine.py); only off the sheet is it lost.
close_reason: What a polishing tip drags is laid where it lifts off, and it is laid back within a pixel or two (BURNISH_LAY 4), so a firm pencil no longer wears a waxed layer away nor leaves blobs where its strokes end.

title: A shading helper: fill an area with strokes as a hand does
description: Shading only looks like pencil when the strokes do what a hand does: side by side at an angle, none quite straight or alike, lighter where the pencil lands and lifts. examples/pencils.py has such a function (shade); make it part of the library, with cross-hatching by shading again at another angle.
close_reason: Sheet.shade, with tests; examples/pencils.py uses it

title: Tips: wear, tilt, the side of a stick, crayon; graphite shine
description: Step 5 of docs/design.md.
notes: Built: tilt (round points), wear (Stick, a tip whose flat grows with the volume laid; sharpen), crayon and oil pastel (crayons.wax, pastels.oil) with resist depending on what is laid over wax (resist_of), and graphite's shine (Medium.sheen, Sheet.shine, render(gloss=...)). Known limits: the side of a stick is the same 5 times its width for every medium (SIDE), which may be too narrow for a long stick of charcoal. A held medium laid over dust (coloured pencil over pastel) ends up under it. A kneaded eraser lifts the unheld share of an oil pastel like dust, which a real one would not. Charcoal over a single firm crayon line still greys it, since one line's film is not yet as slick as it gets (WAX_FULL). Only graphite has sheen: polished wax (burnished coloured pencil, crayon) does not shine yet. A tip pressed hard does not flatten the paper's tooth, so shine still glints on the grain.
close_reason: Tilt, wear, crayon, oil pastel and graphite's shine are built; the limits left are in the notes.

title: Press grows with every pass, so a shading polishes in streaks where its strokes overlap
description: press is summed pass by pass up to 1. With no threshold at all (polish in proportion to pressure), one layer of oil pastel at 0.7 is still polished unevenly from stroke to stroke, about 0.6 of its mean, and 0.55 even at full pressure: the hand's overlaps, stray and +-15% firmness. A pressure flattens wax and fibres to a level set by the load, not by how often it is pressed; press approaching a level set by the bearing would even it out. It shows in the gloss with the lamp overhead, in how wax holds against an eraser, and in the relief. Found doing fusain-bre, whose soft onset took the unevenness from 0.78 to 0.58 (coloured pencil at 0.6) and could do no more.

title: A light ballpoint line's blob is as wide as a firm line's
description: blot's radius is BLOB_WIDE * (radius + 0.5) at any pressure, while a light line is narrower. Since fusain-43t the volume of a blob follows the pressure of the line, but its width does not.

title: A ballpoint drop inks all of a pixel that holds a pass of ink, however small the drop
description: blot sets inked = max(inked, min(total ink / full, 1)) from the pixel's total ink, not the drop's. So any drop, however small, makes a partly inked pixel of a heavy line fully inked and closes its white specks. This is what moved pixels by up to half their tone when the invisible drops of a gently curving line went (fusain-azn).

title: Sheet.rub draws a seed for each stretch it rubs, so where its pressure is zero shifts every later mark's grain
description: rub() splits each pass into runs where pressure > 0 and calls _rub once per run, and each call draws an integer from sheet._rng. So the number of draws depends on the zeros of the pressure field: a drawing whose rub pressure comes from what it measured, or that is changed slightly, re-seeds every stroke after it, and the whole picture's grain changes. Drawing one seed per pass, or per rub, and deriving the runs' seeds from it would make the sheet's random sequence independent of the pressure. examples/lake.py works around it with a pressure floor (LIGHTEST_RUB). Found doing fusain-098.

title: Strokes and rubs twice as fast again, with documented numba options only
description:
The private options _nrt=False and forceinline=True were taken out (the user does not want fusain to rely on undocumented options); inline="always" is in their place. That costs a factor of 1.4 to 2.0 on strokes and 1.2 to 1.8 on rubs against the private options (1120x820: HB 1.48 -> 2.37 s, finger rub 1.97 -> 3.52 s, stump 3.55 -> 4.41 s, 2000 short strokes 0.41 -> 0.78 s).

The cost is numba counting a reference to each array a kernel passes to a helper, per pixel. Win it back with public options only: fold the per-pixel helpers into their kernels by hand, or pass them numbers (or one packed row) and not arrays, or hoist what they read out of the pixel loop. Measure with tools/benchmark.py; the fingerprint must stay identical. Mind ruff's complexity cap of 13 and that _engine.py stays readable. Also measure the cold compile time, which inline="always" may have lengthened.

title: Faster strokes at the cost of the picture
description: What fusain-14p left because it would change the picture (rough estimates): tip steps of width/4 instead of width/8, about 1.8x on stroke and rub kernels; laying once per pixel per stroke instead of about nine times, 3 to 4x on the stroke kernel; a cheaper reach curve than pow(x, 0.6), about 10%; pigment stored by id instead of 24 bands per layer, rubs 2x or more and about 6x less memory, but a different mixing model; threads over tiles in a fixed order. Still exact and not done: fold the gathers and the blend of a render into the kernels (about 25% of a render); vectorise the per-row geometry pass (10 to 15% of a stroke). Also: examples/stilllife.py spends about 80 of its 82 s in its own planning code.
notes: Done, with no change to the picture: examples/stilllife.py plans in half the time (67 s -> 31 to 35 s; the cloth's folds in a compiled kernel, only the cells with a target weighed). Folding the gathers and the blend of a render into the kernels and vectorising the per-row geometry pass go with fusain-95m. What is left here changes the picture and needs a decision: tip steps of width/4, laying once per pixel per stroke, a cheaper reach curve, pigment stored by id, threads over tiles.

title: Move to murex: dense points of a Path computed once, and a compiled km_layer over a ground per pixel
description: Found doing fusain-14p. (1) A murex Path recomputes its dense points on every call (sample() and length each call _dense()); fusain works around it with sheet._Dense, through the _dense subclass hook. Path sampling is about 0.4 ms a stroke and dominates short strokes (37,000 strokes in lake.py: about 15 s); compiling the spline sampling would help. (2) km_layer has no compiled path for a ground per pixel (_km_layer_batch takes one ground), so fusain carries its own copy (km_depth, km_over in _engine.py), pinned bit for bit to sp.km_layer by tests/test_exact.py. Both belong in murex; a change to murex's numbers is a breaking change there and oilpaint must be checked.
close_reason: murex 0.2.0 has both; fusain requires it and its _Dense is gone

title: The ball blots at every point of a gently curving line
description: roll_stroke calls blot whenever drop > 1e-9, which a tiny turn satisfies, so nearly every step lays an invisible drop: about 29% of the pen's time. A threshold tied to what shows would change pictures slightly and take about 25% off the pen kernel.
close_reason: A drop stays on the rim until the line has turned far enough to show (BALL_SHOWS); hatching 0.350 -> 0.286 s, pen over graphite 0.492 -> 0.329 s; nothing is lost

title: An eraser does not smear wax, and coloured pencil leaves no stain
description: In life a vinyl eraser smears a burnished dark and always leaves a tint. In the model the last of a light layer comes off cleanly and nothing is smeared. Also: a white or light pencil pressed hard burnishes only as an ordinary pencil (Medium.melts is 1 for the blender only), and the knife does not touch ballpoint ink.

title: Erasing or scraping polished wax leaves press as it was
description: The tooth stays level after the wax that levelled it is gone (eraser, tools.KNIFE, tools.SAND_ERASER), so what is drawn there next touches the whole pixel.

title: Under the default lamp the gloss of polished wax greys burnished darks, patchily
description: WAX_SHEEN 0.025 at about 0.9 of the lobe adds about +10 L to a burnished black (L 9 to 19), and it follows the unevenness of press stroke by stroke. examples/macaw.py is rendered with gloss=0 to avoid it. Related: the burnish threshold makes press patchy.
close_reason: The gloss of wax is narrow (WAX_SHININESS 5 -> 80): a burnished black under the default lamp L* 18.1 -> 10.3 (matte 6.8), as glossy as before with the lamp overhead; examples/macaw.py is rendered with its gloss again

title: Examples that look at the sheet redraw on any engine change
description: examples/lake.py and the like measure the sheet as they draw, so a tone change of a few thousandths gives a different drawing (different trees), which makes before/after comparison of those pictures noisy. Make them deterministic against small tone changes (e.g. calibrate on a scratch sheet, quantise the feedback).
close_reason: examples/lake.py was the only example steered by what it saw; marks are now scattered over fixed places and fade in with the need, so a tone change of 0.3% moves 0.001% of pixels by more than 8/255 (was 18%)

title: A flattened patch keeps pits in its relief
description: press means level with the peaks, so valleys the lead never reached stay at their old depth beside a plateau in surface_height. In life the peaks come down towards the valleys.
close_reason: surface_height is tooth * (1 - press): a pressed patch is level with its valleys. Six firm layers of 4H: spread of heights 0.210 -> 0.029, pits deeper than a quarter of a tooth 6.3% -> none

title: The burnish threshold makes press patchy
description: press is raised only above a pressure of 0.6, so around 0.6 to 0.75 some strokes cross the threshold and others do not. Wax gloss now shows it as faint streaks, e.g. in the navy oil-pastel ground of examples/output/crayons.png. Squaring press in the gloss mitigates it; a soft onset is the proper fix.
close_reason: Polish and flattening set in by degrees from a pressure of 0.4 (firmness, BURNISH_SOFT), exactly the old law from 0.8: unevenness of press on two crossed layers at 0.6, dark coloured pencil 0.78 -> 0.58, oil pastel 1.08 -> 0.73; firm pressure does what it did

title: A tip narrower than a groove skips it
description: A fine point drawn along an indented line (Sheet.dent) should follow it down, but the model does not know the groove's width, so every stick is treated as riding on the paper either side. Found doing fusain-dyh.

title: A pen in the hand: gathered ink carries from stroke to stroke
description: The blob where a ballpoint lands is a random draw per stroke, not what the previous stroke gathered. A pen in the hand, as Stick is for a medium and Smudger for a tool, would carry the gathered ink over. Also: black ink bronzes grey, where a real black ballpoint bronzes violet or copper.
close_reason: HeldPen keeps the ink its ball gathers from stroke to stroke, until wipe(); ink is conserved; Pen.bronze, and black ink bronzes as its violet does

title: A smudge, an erase or a ballpoint pass is weak where it lands and lifts
description: lay_stroke now gives the paper under the tip where it lands and lifts what it would have had if the tip had slid on and off (put_down, fusain-lgg). rub_stroke (stumps, fingers, erasers) and roll_stroke (ballpoint) still have the old ramp: half strength at the end of a path, fading over a tip width. Also untested: a flat end on a sharply curving end of a path.
notes: The ballpoint half is done (roll_stroke: ink half a pixel behind the landing 0.28 -> 1.04 of the middle's; a dot is 0.91 to 1.0 as dark as a line, from 0.09). Left: rub_stroke, and the test of a flat end on a sharply curving end of a path.

title: The side of a stick bears evenly across its length
description: A stick on its side still marks with an elliptical footprint, so the band fades towards its edges, where a real flat stick of charcoal or pastel lies even across its length. Found doing fusain-3z1.

title: The wax of smeared oil pastel paste stays where it was laid
description: held[IW] counts the wax at a pixel wherever it lies. When a finger moves oil pastel paste (Sheet.paste) the wax does not follow: the smear is not slick and the place it left stays slick.

title: Burnishing does not drag a film that lies over dust
description: burnish() polishes and drags only held; a film (Sheet.film, a waxy medium laid over dust) in the two layers is neither smeared along nor laid into the valleys by a firm pass.

title: A pencil line drawn over pastel dust shows under it
description: The held share of a dry medium (graphite, charcoal pencil) goes in the tooth, under the dust, so a graphite line over a light opaque pastel shows only as a ghost. fusain-ck0 fixed this for waxy media only (Sheet.film); extending the rule to dry media would put most of a second graphite layer on the first one's dust and break the graphite calibrations, so it needs its own design.

title: A stump lays dust on wax as on paper
description: rub_stroke lays what a tool carries on any pixel, waxed or not. Charcoal smeared across a crayon line greys it, where on wax it would hardly cling. Visible in the third row of examples/output/crayons.png where the stump crosses the crayon lines. Found fixing fusain-8nq.

title: A finger carries dust too far: a rubbed join of two pastels is one flat mix
description: Found doing fusain-6lr, once a tool in the hand (Smudger) kept its load. Rubbing a finger to and fro across the join of an orange and a blue soft pastel (examples/colour.py, examples/fixative.py, the same with oil pastel in examples/crayons.py) gives one even olive over the whole width rubbed, with no passage from one colour to the other: tried at pressures 0.3 to 0.6, 9 to 36 passes, passes 44 to 110 px long with a finger 22 wide, all flat. In examples/broadway.py a finger rubbed to and fro over the far fronts and the sky brought the colour of the fronts all over the sky (worked around: pulls from the sky down, with a bare finger). Cause: where it bears a tool lifts about two thirds of the loose dust in a pass into its load, and lays the load back so slowly that it travels far: a loaded 10 px stump on bare paper leaves a trail whose pigment halves every 40 px (4 widths), and a finger carries a colour 2 to 4 of its widths. A real finger smears most of the dust within a fraction of its width and carries only a small share further, so a rubbed join is a gradient a width or two wide. Wanted: most of what is lifted laid back close by (the dust on the face of the tool, as spread_dust does), a small share carried far; judged by the width of the gradient across a rubbed join, and by the trail of a stump dragged out of a tone (tests/test_dust.py pins that one). Related and not modelled either: a stump that has been used for long stays grey and tones lightly for a long time; here one load is spent in about twenty widths.

title: A stump or finger starts every pass clean
description: Found drawing examples/lake.py. Each Sheet.smudge pass, and each pass of Sheet.rub, starts with a tool that carries nothing and takes what it lifted away with it at the end. So: (1) where a pass lands on a tone it lifts a pale dot, visible as dotted rows along the edge of a rubbed area; (2) rubbing a dark tone many times lightens it steadily (about 200 overlapping finger drags through a reflection took it from 124 to 198), where a real stump is soon loaded and gives back as much as it takes; (3) a loaded stump cannot be used to draw a pale tone on bare paper, which is a standard pencil technique. Wanted: a tool in the hand that keeps its load from pass to pass (as Stick is a medium in the hand), cleaned on request; Sheet.rub should carry the load across its own passes. Reproduction of (2): s=Sheet(300,120,seed=1); s.shade((10,10,290,110),pencils.B8,0.9); s.rub((10,10,290,110),tools.STUMP,0.9) several times and compare the tone.
close_reason: Smudger: a tool in the hand keeps its load from pass to pass; Sheet.rub carries the load across its passes

title: Coloured pencil: the blender barely shows and the eraser hardly lightens a dense dark
description: Reported while drawing examples/macaw.py. (1) pencils.BLENDER burnished over hatched coloured pencil made almost no visible difference at drawing sizes. (2) On a dense #141416 hatch, sheet.erase([(30,30),(30.6,30.4)], tools.ERASER, 1.0, 4.5) lifts about a third of the pigment and the rendered value stays at 0.08, so a glint has to be reserved or needs several passes. (3) Four light passes of lemon (0.4) then two of dark teal (0.6) render (153,195,113), barely darker than the lemon: darks must go first. (3) agrees with the pinned layering tests; (1) and (2) need measuring against what real pencil does before deciding whether they are faults.
close_reason: The blender melts into the layer and closes the flecks; wax holds against an eraser; tools.KNIFE and SAND_ERASER scrape. Light over dark is true to life and pinned.

title: A paper texture between wove and rough: a pebbled tooth for charcoal
description: Found redoing examples/deco.py on a paper without the laid pattern. A real charcoal paper has a pebbled or honeycomb tooth: irregular pits a few pixels across, varying from pit to pit. 'wove' removes all variation larger than about 1.5x the grain, so it reads as fine fibres and a rubbed tone looks salt-and-pepper when enlarged. 'rough' keeps the large-scale variation (it has no equivalent of _no_broad), so at small grain it goes blotchy, like camouflage. Wanted: a texture that keeps only the medium scale (band-passed), usable at grain 3 to 5. Judge on flat charcoal tones and gradients, enlarged.
close_reason: Added the pebbled texture and papers.CHARCOAL

title: Sanded card holds little more pastel than cartridge paper
description: On papers.SANDED, layers of soft pastel at 0.7 take 0.78, 0.56, 0.46, 0.31, 0.31, 0.26, 0.16 of the first; on cartridge 0.70, 0.50, 0.36, 0.25, 0.19, 0.12, 0.12. A real sanded paper takes many more layers than an ordinary one (ten or more against three or four). The room in the tooth depends on depth and bite only, and raising the depth also makes the paper grainier; sanded card may need a way to hold more without being deeper.
close_reason: A Paper has a hold (how much its tooth holds for its depth); papers.SANDED holds 2.5 times what a paper of its depth does. Layers of soft pastel on it take 0.92, 0.78, 0.73, 0.58 of the first and still 0.32 at the twelfth; on cartridge paper 0.70, 0.50, 0.36, 0.25 and 0.07.

title: A stroke has one width and round ends

Wanted: a width that can vary along the stroke (a profile, as pressure has), for strokes that recede in perspective or taper; and flat ends for the side or the end of a stick (car bodies, awnings, the bars of a crossing had to be inset by half a width). Found by the agent drawing examples/broadway.py.
notes: From the Broadway pastel redo: a stroke is weak where it ends, so short strokes (a head, a hand) lose their far half; the workaround was two layers stroked in opposite directions with a fix between.
close_reason: Strokes are full strength to their ends; width and tilt profiles; flat ends.

Vine charcoal at width 7, 4.2 px apart, pressure 0.4, left white streaks between strokes, and a finger or chamois did not close them: rubbing should spread the dust over the bare paper between. Found by the agent drawing examples/deco.py.

title: A stump hardly smooths compressed charcoal
description: Compressed charcoal (binding 0.45) stays as laid under a stump, so smooth darks had to be vine underneath with compressed on top. A stump does blend compressed charcoal in life, less easily than vine. Check what share of it a stump moves, against vine, and decide. Found by the agent drawing examples/deco.py.

title: Ballpoint: blobs of ink and the sheen of heavy ink
description: Two things a real ballpoint does that fusain.pens does not: the ball gathers ink and leaves a blob where a line starts or turns sharply; and heavy layers of ink have a bronze sheen under a lamp (the ink layer carries no sheen, and Sheet.shine looks only at the held layer). The groove the ball presses into the paper is fusain-dyh.
close_reason: The ball gathers ink and leaves blobs at landings and turns; heavy ink bronzes.

title: A firm tip does not flatten or indent the paper
description: press is raised only by burnishing wax, and it means level with the peaks of the tooth. A firm pencil does not flatten the tooth (so graphite's shine still glints on the grain), and there is no way to indent a line below the surface, as a stylus or a ballpoint does, for a pencil shaded over it to skip. Needs a depth-below-surface field, separate from press.
close_reason: A firm dry tip raises press; Sheet.dent and Sheet.indent make a groove a pencil skips; a ballpoint leaves one.

title: Polished wax does not shine
description: Only graphite has sheen. A burnished coloured pencil or a heavy crayon has a waxy gloss under a lamp. Give wax a sheen that grows with press, and check that the colour examples stay believable.
close_reason: Wax has a gloss that grows with press, wherever the wax lies.

title: A kneaded eraser lifts oil pastel like dust
description: The share of an oil pastel that the paper does not hold at once lies in the dust layers, so a kneaded eraser lifts it as it lifts charcoal. A real oil pastel smears under a finger but does not come off on a kneaded eraser; it has to be scraped.
close_reason: What the paper does not hold of an oil pastel is paste: a kneaded eraser lifts 19% of a layer, down from 53%.

title: Charcoal over one firm crayon line still greys it
description: A single firm line of wax crayon lays a film of wax thinner than WAX_FULL, so it is not yet as slick as it gets, and it is pressed level, so charcoal dust lies over all of it: charcoal shaded over the line leaves it as dark as the grainy paper around it. Wax resist with dry media therefore does not show for single lines (it does over three firm layers: tests/test_crayons.py).
close_reason: Wax is fully slick to a dry medium once it covers the tooth: charcoal takes 8% on one firm line, down from 39%.

title: The side of a stick is as wide for every medium
description: A stick held on its side marks a band five times the width of its point (SIDE in _engine.py), whatever it is. That suits a pencil lead; a long stick of charcoal or pastel laid flat marks a band as wide as the stick is long. Let the medium or the Stick say how long its side is.
close_reason: Medium.side and Stick(side=) say how long the side of a stick is.

title: A held medium laid over dust ends up under it
description: The held layer is always rendered under the two dust layers. A coloured pencil or a crayon drawn over pastel or charcoal dust therefore shows under the dust, where in life it lies over it and partly binds it.
close_reason: A waxy medium laid over dust now lies on it as a film and binds part of it. Dry held media are not covered: filed separately.

title: Make strokes faster
description: Shading 1120x820 pixels with an HB of width 6 takes about 2.4 s (2.1 s before colour was added). The time is in lay_stroke's work per pixel under the tip: each pixel is visited by about nine steps of the tip, and each visit hashes three numbers, takes a power and a square root, and loops over the 24 bands. Ideas: a table of the streaks per pass, the jitter once per pixel, fewer steps for wide tips. The drawing must stay byte-identical (tools: a fingerprint of held, under, loose, cover and press).
close_reason: Strokes 1.5 to 2.3 times as fast, rubs and renders 1.8 to 2.9, byte-identical (tools/fingerprint.py). Further gains need the picture to change or work in murex.

title: Calibrate graphite tones against scans of real pencil
description: The constants of fusain/_engine.py were set so that tones land near figures estimated from experience (docs/design.md, One step of a stroke), not measured. Scan swatches of real 4H, HB, 2B and 6B on cartridge paper at a few pressures and numbers of layers, and fit the constants to them.

title: Extras: fixative, hatching helpers, ballpoint pen
description: Step 6 of docs/design.md. Ballpoint needs its own deposit rule: a paste laid at a steady rate.
notes:
Fixative built (Sheet.fix, Sheet.fixed). Hatching helpers: Sheet.shade covers them (angle, spacing, hand). Left: the ballpoint pen. It cannot indent the paper until fusain-dyh gives a depth below the surface.

title: stilllife: compute the cloth's folds once for the table rows, and batch the Python around each traced stroke
description: examples/stilllife.py, with no change to the picture: cloth_part calls folds_at twice at identical (x, z) for the table rows (about 84% of the cloth), so reusing cloth_point's result should save about 2 s of the 31 s; it needs plumbing between cloth_point and cloth_part. Also about 9 s is Python around the compiled _trace (Hatcher.bundle and trace, 218k calls): wrap or batch it. Found doing the no-picture part of fusain-6ru.

title: The ink a ball would gather beyond the most it holds is simply not gathered
description: With a HeldPen, long hatchings keep the rim of the ball at its cap, and the conservation identity (drops on the paper plus ink on the ball = BALL_GATHER times the lines' ink) only holds below it. Acceptable but undocumented: document it, or model where the excess goes.

title: The macaw's feet are in an impossible posture
description: examples/macaw.py: the body and plumage are great, the face is fine and the beak passable; leave those. The feet are in a posture no parrot's could take and must be redrawn in a realistic pose: a macaw's foot is zygodactyl (two toes forward, two back), gripping the perch from both sides, the toes wrapping round it with the claws showing beneath, the legs short and coming down from under the belly feathers. Work from reference photographs of a perched macaw. Very low priority, but it needs doing at some point. Alters one picture: regenerate examples/output/macaw.png.
